summary: Describes using several network paths at once to synchronize clocks, aimed at protocols such as NTP and PTP and at applications that need higher accuracy. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Asking several friends for the time, along different routes, makes a mistake by one less likely. This applies that idea to computer clocks.

questions: improve ntp ptp accuracy with multiple paths
how to improve ntp ptp accuracy
subtitle: Synchronize clocks via multiple network paths to improve accuracy and security.

tldr.problem: Clock synchronization protocols like NTP and PTP depend heavily on the single network path between master and slave. Congestion, asymmetry, or attacks on that path can degrade accuracy.
tldr.mechanism: Run the synchronization protocol simultaneously over multiple diverse paths between the clocks. Each path is identified by a different pair of IP addresses. The slave combines results from all paths into a single accurate time.
tldr.outcome: Multipath synchronization improves accuracy, detects and mitigates man-in-the-middle attacks, and provides fault tolerance. Both single-ended (backward-compatible) and dual-ended variants are defined experimentally.

today: RFC 8039 is published as Experimental. It defines methods for improving clock synchronization via multiple paths without modifying NTP or PTP themselves. The experimental status allows the method to be evaluated in real deployments before any path to standardization.

sections.title: Why Clock Accuracy Matters
sections.content:
The Internet's two main time synchronization protocols are NTP (Network Time Protocol), which has been deployed for decades, and PTP (Precision Time Protocol, defined in IEEE 1588), which is increasingly popular for applications requiring higher precision.

Both protocols synchronize a slave clock to a master clock by measuring round-trip delay and correcting for it. However, this works well only if the network path between master and slave is stable and symmetric (takes the same time in both directions).

Real networks often suffer from variable latency, congestion, and path asymmetry (the return path takes a different amount of time than the forward path). An attacker on the network can manipulate delays to shift the slave's clock. Since clocks are critical to security, financial systems, and precise measurement, this is a serious problem.
sections.eli5: When you set your watch by phone, if the line is noisy or slow, you might get the wrong time. If you ask multiple people via different lines and take the average, you are more likely to be right.

sections.title: The Multipath Idea
sections.content:
The RFC observes that modern IP networks are built with multiple paths. Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing, common in large networks, automatically spreads traffic across different paths to balance load.

The multipath approach uses a simple property: packets sent from different source and destination IP addresses often traverse different physical paths through the network. So instead of running the synchronization protocol once over a single path, run it many times in parallel, each using a different {source, destination} address pair.

The slave uses the destination IP address of received packets to identify which path they came from, computes the delay and time offset for each path separately, then combines all results into a single accurate time.

This works at the network layer and requires no changes to NTP or PTP themselves.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending time requests over one line, send them over several lines at once. Each line might take a different route through the network. If you get good data from most of them, you can ignore the bad one.

sections.title: Single-Ended Multipath (Backward Compatible)
sections.content:
In single-ended multipath, only the slave (or NTP client) is aware that multiple paths are being used. The master does not know and treats each incoming connection as a separate device.

For PTP: The slave presents itself to the network using N different clockIdentity values and N different IP addresses. It sends Signaling messages to request unicast synchronization on each identity. The master responds by sending Sync messages to each of the N identities. The slave identifies which path a message came from by checking which of its N IP addresses received it, computes the delay and offset for each path, and combines them.

For NTP: The client initiates N separate NTP sessions with the server, using N different source IP addresses. The server responds normally, unaware that each address is part of the same client. The client combines the time information from all N responses.

This variant is backward compatible: old masters and servers do not need to change. A single-ended slave can connect to any existing time server.
sections.eli5: A smart clock presents itself as N different devices to the time server. The server sends time to each one separately, not knowing they are all the same clock. The smart clock combines the answers.

sections.title: Dual-Ended Multipath (Full Diversity)
sections.content:
In dual-ended multipath, both master and slave use multiple IP addresses. When a slave sends requests or responses, it can choose which of its IP addresses to send from, and the master receives them from different source addresses.

For PTP: A single clockIdentity is used (so the master knows it is a single slave), but the clock listens on N IP addresses. The slave negotiates unicast connections between each of its N_s addresses and each of the master's N_m addresses. For each {master IP, slave IP} pair, the protocol runs an independent exchange. The slave combines data from all N_s * N_m paths.

For NTP: The client chooses N_svr server addresses and N_c client addresses, initiating N_svr * N_c separate protocol instances. Each instance exchanges time information over one {server, client} address pair.

Dual-ended multipath provides higher path diversity than single-ended because each address pair is more likely to traverse a truly different network path.
sections.eli5: The time server also uses multiple addresses. The smart clock sets up connections between all combinations of its addresses and the server's addresses, so they have the best chance of finding totally different routes.

sections.title: Security and Fault Tolerance
sections.content:
Multiple diverse paths provide three key benefits:

Robustness against delay attacks: An attacker on the network cannot delay your clock by much without delaying most or all paths. A good combining algorithm will ignore or downweight the slow paths.

Fault tolerance: If one path fails, the slave still has the others. The protocol continues running.

Accuracy: Papers referenced in the RFC show that multipath synchronization significantly improves clock accuracy compared to single-path.

However, the RFC notes that paths may partially overlap, so an attacker at a shared router could still affect multiple paths. Additionally, the multipath approach uses more server resources (the master must respond to N times more requests), which could amplify DDoS attacks if not carefully managed.

Path selection is important: IP addresses should be chosen so their paths are as diverse as possible. The RFC discusses using traceroute-based path discovery to filter out redundant address pairs and verify that paths are actually different.
sections.eli5: An attacker cannot slow down your time by much if you are getting time from many different routes. If one route gets blocked, the others still work. This makes time synchronization more secure and reliable.

sections.title: Combining Results and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Once the slave receives time information from all paths, it must combine them into a single accurate time. The RFC does not mandate a specific algorithm; different combining methods have different strengths. Some (like NTP's algorithm) are robust against outliers and attacks. Others (like Kalman filtering) are more resilient to random delay variation.

A key advantage of multipath synchronization is that it can coexist with traditional single-path clocks. A single-ended multipath slave can connect to a conventional time server. A dual-ended multipath master can accept connections from old single-path clients. This backward compatibility allows gradual deployment.

The RFC is experimental and is intended to be evaluated for at least two years to verify that the method works in practice and to identify any operational issues with real-world networks.
sections.eli5: The combining step is flexible: use whatever method works best for your needs. Old clocks still work fine alongside new multipath ones, so you do not have to upgrade everything at once.
